Engineering · Candidate assignment

Work Request
Service

A small software delivery exercise, from specification to a validated GitHub handover.

Audience: Candidates.
Reviewer: @tejnieminen
Submission deadline: Provided at briefing.
Expected effort: 4–6 hours of active work, including tests and documentation.

Deliver a Small Software Solution

A team needs a simple way to record work requests, track their progress and understand how they have changed.

Build a small application that supports this workflow. Choose a language you are comfortable with and expose either a command-line interface or an HTTP API. Both are equally acceptable. Use an AI coding assistant or agent to support the work and explain how you directed and checked it.

We assess your engineering approach, judgement and learning potential. Keep the design proportionate and deliver something another person can run.

Prerequisites: You have access to an AI coding assistant or agent and a GitHub account, and can use them independently to complete and share the assignment.

Define the Work Before Implementing It

Write a short specification covering:

  • Your interpretation of the problem and intended user workflow.
  • Required behaviour and testable acceptance criteria.
  • Data model, assumptions and scope boundaries.
  • A small implementation and validation plan.

Use the requirements below as the starting point. Ask questions when needed; reasonable documented assumptions are acceptable. Update the specification if your understanding changes.

Implement the Core Workflow

Capability Required behaviour
Create a requestAccept a non-empty title, a description and a priority of low, medium or high. Assign a unique ID and initial status new.
Inspect requestsList requests, filter by status and priority, and inspect a request by ID.
Progress workSupport new → in_progress → done. Reject all other status changes in the initial version.
Persist dataPreserve requests and history across application restarts. A local file or SQLite is sufficient.
Show historyRecord creation and successful status changes, including a timestamp and, for transitions, previous and new status. Make the history inspectable.
Handle errorsGive understandable errors for invalid input, an unknown ID or an invalid transition. Rejected operations must leave the stored request and history unchanged.

No particular framework, architecture or storage technology is expected. State remaining assumptions, such as empty descriptions, ordering, timestamp format and combined filter behaviour.

Initial State Model

Example User Journey

  1. Create “Prepare a demo” with priority high.
  2. Find it using a status or priority filter.
  3. Start work and then mark it as done.
  4. Restart the application and confirm the request is still available.
  5. Inspect its creation and status-change history.
  6. Attempt a forbidden transition and verify that no data or history was changed.

Provide runnable commands or API examples for this journey in the README.

Apply One Small Requirement Change

After reaching a working initial version, record it in a Git commit or tag. Then implement this change:

A completed request must be reopenable into in_progress. Reopening requires a non-empty reason, which must be stored in the request history.

This is a planned second step, included in the total time budget. Everyone receives the same change upfront; no additional release or meeting is needed to begin it.

  • Update the specification and acceptance criteria.
  • Implement reopening and validate its rules.
  • Confirm that existing behaviour still works.
  • Record the change in a subsequent commit.
  • Briefly explain what changed in the specification, implementation and tests.

The change allows done → in_progress only when a reason is supplied. Other unsupported transitions remain invalid.

Validate the Result

Include automated tests that cover:

  • Creating and retrieving a request.
  • Listing and filtering.
  • Valid initial transitions and rejected invalid transitions.
  • Persistence after reopening the application or reloading storage.
  • Relevant validation errors and unknown IDs.
  • History entries for successful operations and no mutation on rejected operations.
  • Reopening with a reason and rejecting reopening without a reason.

Choose test boundaries appropriate to your implementation. We value tests that check meaningful behaviour. A coverage percentage target is unnecessary.

Record the commands you actually ran and their outcomes. Clearly separate observed results from proposed future checks. If a test fails or a requirement remains incomplete, disclose it.

Check for Secrets and Personal Data Before Sharing

You are responsible for checking that the repository contains no secrets or personally identifiable information (PII) in its content or committed history before pushing or granting access. Use synthetic data throughout.

Check source code, configuration, examples, tests, stored application data, logs, screenshots, documentation and agent-interaction excerpts. Exclude API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys and real people's personal information. A private repository and .gitignore do not replace this check or remove previously committed content.

Document the check in your working-method description:

  • What you inspected, including tracked files and Git history.
  • Which tools, commands and manual checks you used.
  • What you found, how you resolved findings and what you rechecked.
  • Any limitations of the check. Report results without reproducing sensitive values.

If a real secret was exposed, revoke or rotate it before proceeding and remove it from the shared material and history. Remove any PII before submission. Do not treat a scanner's clean result alone as proof that no personal data exists.

Explain Your Process and Agentic SWE Usage

Provide a concise account of how you moved from the brief to delivery:

  1. What did you plan, and how did you divide the work?
  2. Which technologies, tools, models and agents did you use, and why?
  3. What did you delegate to the assistant or agent? What did you decide or perform yourself?
  4. How did you instruct it, review its output and integrate its changes?
  5. What did you correct or reject, if anything? Otherwise, how did you check the output you accepted?
  6. How did the requirement change affect your plan and solution?
  7. What limitations remain, what did you learn and what would you do next?
  8. How did you check the repository and its history for secrets and PII, what were the results and how did you resolve any findings?

Include 1–2 representative interaction examples or short summaries. A single coding agent is sufficient; multi-agent orchestration is optional and receives no automatic advantage.

Do not include full conversation exports, private reasoning traces or unrelated usage history.

Deliver Through GitHub

Your repository must contain:

Content Minimum expectation
SoftwareSource code and necessary dependency/configuration files.
SpecificationRequirements, acceptance criteria, assumptions and the reopening change.
TestsAutomated checks and instructions for running them.
READMEPrerequisites, setup/run/test commands, example workflow and known limitations.
Working-method descriptionProcess, technology choices, AI/agent usage and handling of the requirement change.
Validation recordChecks executed, results and remaining uncertainties.
Secrets/PII check recordInspection scope, tools/commands, manual review, findings, remediation and recheck results.
Release notesRelease version, date, commit/tag, included functionality, changes, limitations, validation summary and installation instructions.
ReflectionApproximate active time spent, lessons and next steps.

Suggested structure; equivalent organisation is fine:

work-request-service/
├── README.md
├── SPEC.md
├── WORKLOG.md
├── RELEASE_NOTES.md
├── src/
├── tests/
└── dependency/configuration files, if needed

Keep documentation short and factual. Sections may be combined into fewer files.

Release Notes and Installation Instructions

Identify the delivered release with a version and Git tag pointing to the final submission commit. In RELEASE_NOTES.md, record:

  • Release version, date and corresponding tag/commit.
  • What is included, including the reopening change.
  • Known limitations, unfinished requirements and validation results.
  • Installation instructions for this release: prerequisites and versions, how to check out the tag, dependency installation, any configuration or storage initialisation, and commands to start and smoke-test the application.

Make the installation steps directly usable; do not provide only a link to the README. A hosted GitHub Release, binary package and cloud deployment are optional.

Submission Checklist

  • Before pushing or sharing, check content and Git history for secrets and PII, resolve findings and document how the check was performed.
  • Push the software, specification, tests and documentation.
  • Identify the initial working version and the subsequent reopening change in Git history.
  • Check that the README enables someone else to run and test the solution from a clean checkout where practical.
  • Include release notes with release details and installation instructions.
  • Tag the final release and send the repository URL, release tag and final commit SHA.
  • Grant @tejnieminen access to the repository if private; ensure it is accessible for review.
  • Mention any incomplete requirements, failed checks or known limitations.

A private repository is sufficient. Public publication is optional and provides no assessment advantage. Do not include credentials, confidential Qvantel or project information, real customer data or material belonging to another employer.

Keep Scope Proportionate

Aim for 4–6 hours total, including the requirement change, tests and documentation. Stop near the time budget and explain unfinished work. This is a planning guide rather than a speed score.

The following are outside the required scope:

  • Browser UI, authentication, user management and role-based permissions.
  • Cloud hosting, containers and implemented CI/CD.
  • External integrations or an AI feature inside the application.
  • Distributed deployment and concurrent multi-user writes.
  • Production-grade recovery, monitoring or infrastructure.

Manual local validation is sufficient when the commands and results are recorded. Extra features, elaborate architecture, more agents or paid tools receive no automatic credit.

The expected outcome is specified → implemented → validated → delivered through GitHub. Delivery means the reviewer can access the submitted revision and run it using your instructions.

What Happens Next?

Tero reviews the repository for clear scope, ownership, meaningful validation, purposeful AI use and a usable handover. Minor disclosed defects may be acceptable; explain them honestly.

If the work provides sufficient evidence, you will be invited to a 30–45-minute interview to demonstrate the solution and discuss your decisions, tests, agent workflow and lessons learned. No separate algorithm puzzle or mandatory live-coding exercise is planned.

The repository and discussion support the project-assignment decision. You will receive an outcome and development feedback.
